6.33.4.en: He made clear that wisdom is not attained by much talking, but by listening to the wise and acting upon wisdom through the study of the Law.

6.33.5.en: v It was said: "Wisdom is in the understanding of the faithful." Xenocrates, in his treatise on "Intelligence", says that wisdom consists, according to scientific knowledge, first in the causes and in the rational being. He looks at "intelligence" from two sides: the practical and the theoretical, the latter being human wisdom. Therefore wisdom is a kind of intelligence, but not every kind of intelligence is wisdom...

6.33.6.en: Heraclitus attacks human beings who lack faith, saying: "They do not know how to speak and how to listen." Doubtless he drew help from the text: "If you love to hear, you will gain knowledge, and if you incline your ear you will be wise" (cf. Sir 6:33).

6.33.7.en: St. Clement of Alexandria: Stand in the assembly of the elders, and cleave to him who is wise [34].

6.33.8.en: Ben Sirach links the divine commandment with enjoying the experiences of the saints in the Lord. Besides enjoying the commandment of the Lord as a source of wisdom, he advises his disciples to choose good friends. For friendship or fellowship with the wise has its effect on a person. "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed" (Prov 13:20).

6.33.9.en: Be ready to hear every divine discourse, and do not let the proverbs of understanding escape you [35].

6.33.10.en: The need for the law of God, the source of wisdom. This is what distinguishes wisdom full of godliness from philosophical wisdom.

6.33.11.en: And if you see a man of understanding, rise early to him, and let your steps wear out the threshold of his door [36].

6.33.12.en: He who desires to learn wisdom must frequent the places of the wise, and whenever he hears of one of the wise he must go to him and visit his door until his feet become familiar with the thresholds of his door.

6.33.13.en: St. Augustine sees that the man of understanding here is the Lord of glory Jesus. He asks us to rise early to Him and cleave to Him and ask Him: "Master, where dwellest thou?" (Jn 1:38), so that we may abide with Him all the days of our life.

6.33.14.en: In St. John Chrysostom's discourse on the eunuch, the minister of Candace queen of Ethiopia (Acts 8:30-31), who longed to understand what Isaiah the prophet had said, he says: [He showed us virtue in his conduct by his invitation (to Philip): he was a pagan minister sitting in his chariot, and he called a man lesser than himself in appearance, wearing despised clothing, to come up and ride with him. Do you see his zealous spirit? Do you see his surpassing devotion? Do you see a God-fearing pagan fulfilling the saying of the wise man: "If thou seest a man of understanding, get thee betimes unto him, and let thy foot wear the steps of his door" (cf. Sir 6:36)? Do you not see how he became worthy not to be slighted? Do you not see how he became worthy to receive a privilege from on high? Do you not see that he neglected nothing on his part? Therefore through his teacher he received a distinguished knowledge of the effect of what is written in the Holy Bible, and light shone upon his mind[27].]

6.33.15.en: St. Augustine sees that this saying explains what is stated in verse 34, namely the endeavor to cleave to the wise. He gave us an example in the Lord Christ's call to Peter and Andrew (Mt 4:19). They followed Him and did not leave Him; they asked Him: "Where dwellest thou?" (Jn 1:38), and He disclosed to them where He dwelt[28].

6.33.16.en: Think on the ordinances of the Lord, and practice His commandments, for He strengthens your mind at all times, and the desire for wisdom is given to you [37].

6.33.17.en: He ends this chapter by affirming the role of our Lord Jesus in enjoying true friendship: 1. Meditation on the ordinances of the Lord, or the divine commandment, lifts the believer's heart as it were to heaven, and he sees that its constitution is true love; God Himself is love. "And we have known and believed the love that God hath to us. God is love; and he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him" (1 Jn 4:16). And we come into touch with the heavenly orders who glorify God for His love for mankind and His wonderful work on the Cross for their salvation. 2. By practicing His commandments in our daily life we taste the sweetness of friendship with God and the heavenly orders and with one another. 3. The Lord establishes our mind at all times, so that events cannot shake our friendship, but develop it and make it firm. 4. The Lord gives us the desire for wisdom, as He sanctifies our will so that it is in harmony with His divine will.

6.34.s.en: Shine upon me with the light of Your love, that I may cleave to You, O Friend of mankind

6.34.0.en: v How my soul longed to meet You in the garden of Eden with Adam and Eve.

6.34.1.en: I hear Your voice as You walk in the garden, and I feel that I am carried on Your arms!

6.34.2.en: Heaven is not far off; even the wild beasts seek my friendship, for I am Your beloved and Your friend.

6.34.3.en: My first parents accepted the counsel of the enemy of good, so rebellion took possession of my heart, and my friendship with You turned into enmity!

6.34.4.en: Even the heavenly orders stood in amazement at what I did, I who am dust and ashes!

6.34.5.en: Disgrace and shame came upon me, my nature was corrupted, and corruption settled in my depths!

6.34.6.en: Darkness settled in my heart, and enmity entered with it!

6.34.7.en: v In Your love You came down to me, and by Your Cross You planted me by the streams of living water.

6.34.8.en: I have come to suffer a struggle within me.

6.34.9.en: Will the first friendship return, and my will be in harmony with Your holy will?

6.34.10.en: By Your grace You gave me sonship, and established Your Kingdom within me.

6.34.11.en: You poured Your meekness into me, that I may draw my brethren by sweet speech and a gentle tongue.

6.34.12.en: You made me a member of Your Church, so that those who are at peace with me became many.

6.34.13.en: But among the thousand, I find You a faithful and mighty counselor.

6.34.14.en: v Friendship has been corrupted in the world, and there is the friend who seeks what is for his own benefit.

6.34.15.en: And there is one who befriends me in the time of ease, and ignores me in the day of distress.

6.34.16.en: He exerts all his effort, not to support me but to hinder my steps.

6.34.17.en: v You are the faithful Friend, my strong refuge.

6.34.18.en: You are my eternal treasure and the medicine of life; in place of earthly things You give me heavenly things.

6.34.19.en: And in place of corruption You give me immortality and incorruption.

6.34.20.en: You establish Your Kingdom within me, and You have become nearer to me than my father and mother.

6.34.21.en: Your commandment gives me an easy and sweet yoke?

6.34.22.en: You grant me to walk in Your company, O Crucified One; I set out on the narrow way to the crown of joy!

6.34.23.en: You turn the fetters of the commandment into precious ornaments with which my soul is adorned.

6.34.24.en: v With every morning I sing of Your new mercies.

6.34.25.en: You shine upon me with the light of Your knowledge and Your mysteries.

6.34.26.en: You teach me and train me, and I become wise in You.

6.34.27.en: In You my mind will not be shaken, but increases in understanding, wisdom and knowledge.

6.34.28.en: You carry me from victory to victory, and from glory to glory.

6.34.29.en: You prepare me as a heavenly bride sitting at Your right hand, O King of kings and Lord of lords.

6.34.30.en: Glory to You, O Wisdom of God, for You became incarnate for me and for all my brethren.

6.34.31.en: Appendix to Sirach 6: A faithful friend is the medicine of life (Sir 6:16). 1. The need for a friend: Who are the friends whom the sweet voice of the Crucified drew, if not the believers from all the nations? And who are those at peace with us, if not the heavenly orders who rejoice in our salvation.

6.34.32.en: "A faithful friend is a strong refuge, and he who has found one has found a treasure. A faithful friend has no equal, and there is none who can weigh his loftiness. A faithful friend is the medicine of life, and those who fear the Lord will find him" (6:14-16). 2. Sincere friendship: St. Augustine says: ["A faithful friend is the medicine of life" (cf. Sir 6:16). There is no remedy so effective in healing pains as the sincere friend who comforts you in your afflictions, manages you in your problems, rejoices in your success and grieves in your calamities. He who has found such a friend has found a treasure. For the faithful friend has no like, and the weight of gold and silver does not equal the goodness of his faithfulness (cf. Sir 6:14-15).] 3. Friendship and the fear of the Lord: He who carries the fear of the Lord in his heart, and walks in the spirit of godliness in the wisdom of the Spirit, obtains good friendship even with the heavenly orders. 4. Friendship with wisdom herself: "My son, choose instruction from your youth, and you will find wisdom in your old age. Come to her like the plowman and the sower, and wait for her good harvest, for you will labor a little in her work, and will eat of her fruit soon" (6:18-19). 5. Care to preserve friendship: St. John Chrysostom says: [Let us follow love, for it is a safety valve that does not allow us to suffer any evil. Let us bind ourselves to one another. Let there be no deceit among us and no lie, for where friendship is, there is nothing of the kind. Another wise man tells us this: "Though thou drewest a sword at thy friend, yet despair not: for there may be a returning to favour. If thou hast opened thy mouth against thy friend, fear not; for there may be a reconciliation: except for upbraiding, or pride, or disclosing of secrets, or a treacherous wound: for for these things every friend will depart" (cf. Sir 22:21-22).] 6. False friends: St. Ephrem the Syrian says: [If you have a friendship with one of the brethren and harm comes to you because of your association with him, hasten and cut yourself off from him. I do not say this to you, beloved, so that you may hate people, no. But so that you may cut off the causes of vice.]

7.0.0.en: 1 Do not do evil, and evil will not overtake you. 2 Keep away from the unrighteous, and the unrighteous will turn away from you. 3 My son, do not sow in the furrows of iniquity, lest you reap it sevenfold.

7.0.1.en: The only holy Friend, who is able to dwell in our hearts and establish His Kingdom in them, is the Lord of glory Jesus. He reigns over the heart, so the enemy of good finds no place in us, and flees from us. In this way evil or iniquity has no authority over our hearts or minds or emotions, but our depths are turned into a sanctuary for the Lord. We are sanctified by divine grace, and we draw many to enjoy divine friendship, and friendship with human beings in the Lord.

7.0.2.en: This is on the side of the holy and mighty divine Friend; yet He does not storm our life by force, but grants us to have our own part, which reveals our desire for the holy life. It is fitting for us to seek holiness and strive with a spirit of vigilance, so that we expel every evil thought and seek to acquire the holy thought. For evil does not impose itself on us.

7.0.3.en: v Those who strive to have a virtuous life and a life of love for God must give up self-reliance and all empty vainglory. They must also strive for the reformation of their life and their hearts.

7.1.0.en: The steadfast mind that loves God is a guide and a way to God[2].

7.2.0.en: v He who is purified from evil and sin is called a saint. For the absence of evil from a person is a greater perfection of the soul and pleases God greatly[3].

7.2.1.en: St. Anthony the Great: Moreover the Holy Bible has drawn for us the way of perfection by presenting negative commandments and positive ones, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit of God.

7.2.2.en: v The (first) Psalm draws for us the way of virtue, with knowledge and art, for withdrawal from evil is the beginning of good; if you seek perfect virtue from the beginning, you turn back before you begin, but the Psalm prepares the way for us so that we may face it with courage.

7.2.3.en: I believe that growth in the love of God is like the ladder that the blessed Jacob once saw, which on one side was on the earth, and on the other side was rising toward the virtuous life, where a person begins by climbing the first rungs of the ladder, and afterward rises to a higher rung with deliberation and patience until he reaches what human nature can attain. So, by climbing the first rungs of the ladder we rise above the earth, to practice the life that God wants for us. And the beginning of progress is withdrawal from evil, where such withdrawal is as easy as "Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not steal" (Ex 20:13-15); this does not require positive action. But when we are asked for that commandment: "Love thy neighbor as thyself", "sell that thou hast, and give to the poor" (Mt 19:21), "whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain" (Mt 5:41), these works are done by the wrestler who has experienced strength through divine wisdom, and through small works he leads us to perfection.

7.3.0.en: For he sets before us three things that we must avoid: walking in the counsel of the wicked, standing in the way of sinners, and sitting in the seat of the scornful. This order begins with taking the decision and then carrying it out; the beginning here is in the pure thought, for the foundation of the works of the flesh springs from purity of heart, and adultery begins in the lustful soul and ends in adultery of the body, so the Lord said: "Those things which defile a man come out of the heart" (cf. Mt 15:18)[4].

7.3.1.en: v Question: How can a person come to hate sins (Ps 119:163)?

7.4.0.en: Answer: Hatred rises in people from hateful and grievous events toward those who cause such disturbance. Therefore if someone is thoroughly convinced of the gravity of the many evils that sins cause, he spontaneously, without anyone urging him, and by an inward inclination, experiences hatred for them, as the psalmist showed: "I hate and abhor lying" (cf. Ps 119:163)[5].

7.4.1.en: v Question: How is the soul fully convinced that God forgives it its sins?

7.4.2.en: Answer: When it observes within itself the inclination of him who said: "I hate and abhor lying" (Ps 119:163). When God sent His only-begotten Son for the forgiveness of our sins, He forgives them to us as long as we believe in His role.

7.5.0.en: St. David sings of mercy and judgment (Ps 101:1), and testifies that God is merciful and just (Ps 115:5), so it is necessary that there enter into us what the prophets and apostles say in the passages concerning repentance, that the judgments of God's righteousness (Ps 119:62) are manifest, and His mercy is perfect in forgiving sins[6].

7.5.1.en: St. Basil the Great: Do not do evil, and evil will not take hold of you [1].

7.5.2.en: Evil does not impose itself on a person; rather it is the person who seeks it, and he who plants the seed of evil in its furrows, then iniquity multiplies and gains authority over him.

7.5.3.en: Iniquity is merely a seed; when a person plants it, it becomes a weak plant that grows with time and becomes a mighty tree, and then he reaps sevenfold. He who sows evil reaps evil multiplied. An example is the troubles that came upon the household of King David, which were the fruit of the evil he committed with Bathsheba (2 Sam 12:9-12). With every slackness toward sin, it gains the right to break into our depths with more power. And with every refusal of the deception of the enemy, the soul increases in boldness, strength and authority over the devil and his wiles and works.

7.5.4.en: It is fitting for the believer to be faithful in the uprightness of his life, not making light of evil and receiving it in his mind or heart or inner feelings, as in his words and outward conduct. Let his life be in Christ, whether personal, family or public. Let him not seek success or gain or fame at the expense of his principles in the Lord.

7.5.5.en: v Depart from evil, and evil itself will depart from you. Do not sow the seed of evil deeds in the furrow of injustice, so that you will not reap it multiplied sevenfold... Do not say: "His mercies are great, He will forgive the multitude of my sins"...

7.6.0.en: It is stated in Proverbs: "His own iniquities shall take the wicked himself, and he shall be holden with the cords of his sins. He shall die without instruction; and in the greatness of his folly he shall go astray" (Prov 5:22-23)[7].

7.7.0.en: Fulgentius: v Those who fully understand that all their work must aim at attaining the good life, and yet are distracted by temporal blessings; these I liken to people who seek a cure and medicine but do not know how to use it, and are not troubled about (their ignorance of using it). Therefore let us not excuse our sins that we commit by the pretext of the circumstances of the environment or by attributing them to another person, but let us lay the blame on ourselves. For if our souls surrender willingly to sloth, they cannot escape defeat[8].

7.8.0.en: v He who advances in a godly life does not allow evil to enter his soul, and when his soul is freed from evil, he is in peace and safety. And wicked demons or sudden accidents have no authority over him, but God delivers him from every evil, and he lives under invisible protection, because he is a lover of God. If someone praises such a person, he does not care about it, and if someone reviles him, he does not defend himself against his reviler, nor is he angered at any of his sayings[9].

7.8.1.en: St. Anba Anthony the Great: v He who flees from worldly pleasures and passions becomes an impregnable tower against the demon of murmuring. For murmuring is caused by the feeling of deprivation of some pleasures that exist or are expected. We cannot overcome it as long as we are bound with earthly bonds. Whenever Satan looks at us and sees us bound by them, he sets his nets for us to stir up murmuring in us.

7.8.2.en: Father Evagrius the monk: Keep away from iniquity, and it will turn away from you [2].

7.8.3.en: My son, do not sow in the furrows of iniquity, and you will not reap it sevenfold [3].

7.8.4.en: Keeping away from iniquity and fleeing from it carries a spirit of strength, because the enemy of good asks us to enter into dialogue with him so as to cast deception into our hearts as he did with Eve. He who goes of his own free will to the furrows of iniquity, and there sows a small plant of iniquity, this planting grows and multiplies, and is not easily uprooted after it has been planted. For the seed of iniquity sprouts and grows until it becomes a tree that is hard to uproot. When we open the door to the enemy, he enters and then storms the place of the steering wheel, and drives us wherever he wishes.

7.9.s.en: 2. Divine love and fitting conduct in public affairs

7.9.0.en: 4 Do not seek of the Lord a place of leadership, nor of the king a seat of glory. 5 Do not claim to be righteous before the Lord, nor wise before the king. 6 Do not seek to become a judge, lest you be unable to root out injustice; perhaps you will fear the face of the mighty, and so put a stumbling block in the way of your uprightness. 7 Do not sin against the assembly of the city, and do not cast yourself down among the crowd. 8 Do not return to sin a second time, for you will not be held guiltless of the first. 9 Do not be fainthearted in your prayer. 10 And do not neglect almsgiving.

7.9.1.en: Do not seek of a lord a place of leadership, nor of a king a seat of honor [4].

7.9.2.en: The heavenly Friend calls us not to seek the chief seats, and also warns us against the love of leadership, so that we may not be distracted from our salvation by a spirit of pride. The Lord Christ says: "When thou art bidden of any man to a wedding, sit not down in the highest room; lest a more honourable man than thou be bidden of him; And he that bade thee and him come and say to thee, Give this man place; and thou begin with shame to take the lowest room" (Lk 14:8-9). It is fitting for the believer not to rely on his own understanding or his own abilities, nor to seek temporal honor, so that he seeks neither vain glories nor temporal authority, nor justifies himself before God. The divine Friend came down from heaven and took the last ranks of humanity, becoming the crucified servant between two thieves, stirring in us a spirit of rivalry to hasten toward Him that we may take the last ranks with Him.

7.10.0.en: Do not declare yourself righteous before a lord, nor show yourself wise before a king [5].

7.10.1.en: Through the divine friendship, what occupies us when we stand before a lord or a king is not to display our righteousness or our wisdom, but that our conduct bear witness to the righteousness of Christ and His divine wisdom. The wise man commands us: "Put not forth thyself in the presence of the king, and stand not in the place of great men: For better it is that it be said unto thee, Come up hither; than that thou shouldest be put lower in the presence of the prince whom thine eyes have seen" (Prov 25:6-7). It is not wise for a man to justify himself before God, because all have sinned (Ps 143:2; Rom 3:9-10). And as the psalmist says: "If You judge, who will be justified before You?" And it is foolish for a man to boast of wisdom before the king or ruler, because it is hard to perceive what is in his intentions (Prov 25:3).

7.10.2.en: The judge has a serious obligation to root out evil by persisting in resisting the powers of evil (Lev 19:15).

7.11.0.en: v Nothing generates haughtiness like a good conscience when we are not careful. Therefore, since Jesus knows that if we do anything faithfully this tendency rises in us, He said to His disciples: "When ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants" (Lk 17:10)... And Solomon also says: "Do not justify yourself before the Lord"[10].

7.11.1.en: St. John Chrysostom: Do not seek to become a judge, if you are not able to root out iniquity.

7.11.2.en: Lest you show deference to the presence of the mighty man, and make concessions of your integrity [6].

7.11.3.en: In the Hebrew text it is: "to become a ruler".

7.12.0.en: v "Seek not to be made a judge, being not able to take away iniquity" (cf. Sir 7:6). Much more we say here: "Do not seek to be a teacher, if you are not qualified for the dignity of this office, and even if you are drawn into it, refuse it[11].

7.12.1.en: St. John Chrysostom: v We do not advise you to leave him who entrusted you with the care of the holy churches of God (2 Cor 11:28), but we ask you to take care of yourself in the fear of the Lord. Do not accept gifts from anyone (Prov 15:27), and do not be crooked in judgment (Sir 20:29). Do not be ashamed before a man of authority, and do not acquit the guilty or condemn the innocent (Susanna 53) LXX. Flee from covetousness, the root of all evil (1 Tim 6:10), which in truth has been called a kind of idolatry (Eph 5:5). And do not be proud, that you may be a disciple of the Apostle who said: "Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate" (Rom 12:16). Do not try to please men, for you know with whom those who did so ended; they became strangers to the service of Christ. Indeed the Apostle says: "If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10). And submit to the Lord who says: "Learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls" (Mt 11:29).

7.13.0.en: Quench anger and put it away from you, for it is destructive to a person. Do everything according to the counsel of God, and you will find Him a helper to you. Always fear death, for it is coming upon us all. Remember the hour of your departure, and do not sin against God. If you reach the point of quietness, you will find rest and grace wherever you decide to withdraw[12].

7.13.1.en: Sts. Barsanuphius and John: Do not sin against the inhabitants of a city, and do not humiliate yourself before the people [7].

7.13.2.en: It is fitting for the believer to work for the building up and salvation of the community, and not to shatter his energies and deviate from his mission toward it, lest he humiliate himself before the crowd, especially on the great day of the Lord.

7.13.3.en: Do not repeat your sin, for you will be punished even for (the sin of) one [8].

7.13.4.en: Among the traits of him who despises God's long-suffering, makes light of his brother's love, and ignores the building up of the community is that he sins against God, the salvation of his soul and the edification of his brethren, and after repenting of what he has committed he returns and repeats the error.

7.13.5.en: Even in our dealings with leaders or rulers, we may err because of our human weakness and the Lord covers us, but if we become lax and repeat the fall, the Lord lifts His hand from us, and our first sins, which the Lord covered in order to rescue us from the hands of the leaders, are exposed, and we are called to account for the former and later errors! If God does not discipline us when we sin once, that is not a reason for repeating sin in reliance upon His long-suffering. God does not condemn us because we have sinned, but condemns us if we do not repent after we have sinned, and this is confirmed by our repeating the sin in slackness. One of the desert Fathers says: "I do not remember that the demons led me astray twice in a single matter."

7.14.0.en: v He who is disciplined for his former sins and obtains forgiveness, let him prepare himself for a wrath more severe than the first if he sins again... "Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee" (Jn 5:14)[13].

7.14.1.en: v Question: What must one do who repents of a sin and then falls again into the same sin?

7.14.2.en: Answer: He who repented once and committed the same sin again, let him first be convinced before himself that he has not removed the chief cause of the sin, as from a corrupt root, and so necessarily the same evils sprout again. He is like one who wishes to cut off the branches of a tree, leaving the root as it is, and since the root remains stored in the earth, the same (sin) sprouts again to a lesser degree. Therefore, since there are certain sins whose origin is not in themselves but which proceed from other sins, he who wants to purify himself entirely from sin must cut off the very first causes of those sins. For example, strife and envy (Rom 13:13) do not spring from themselves, but from the root of haughtiness and love of (vain) glory; so he who seeks glory from men competes with one who has great fame surpassing his own, and envies him for it.

7.15.0.en: Therefore he who falls into the vice of envy or strife, and returns and falls into it again, let him realize that the primary cause is the love of glory of which we spoke before. In this let him take care of this sickness, for he needs to be healed of it, and that by its opposite, that is, by humility, performing simple services, practicing humility. In this way, once he is established in the virtue of humility, he does not fall again into the products of haughtiness and love of glory[14].

7.16.s.en: 3. Between divine love and worship in a spirit of godliness

7.16.0.en: 11 Do not say: "God will look upon the multitude of my offerings, and when I offer them to the Most High He will accept them."

7.16.1.en: Our heavenly Friend does not need a multitude of offerings, nor of prayers and almsgiving; rather He smells in the offerings the incense of holiness and purity. And He delights in the fervent heart rejoicing in love in prayer, and in offering the sweet word with joy along with every gift or alms. The way of godliness is not impossible, but by love for God in earnestness we enjoy the virtuous life.

7.17.0.en: v It is fitting for us not to say that it is impossible for a person to walk in the virtuous life, but to say of it that it is not easy. Truly (the virtuous life) is not obtained by all in equal measure, since only the devout who have a mind that loves God obtain it. The ordinary mind is earthly and changeable, out of which come good thoughts and evil thoughts, and it is variable, inclined toward material things, but the mind that loves God shatters the evil that comes to human beings because of their unintentional negligence[15].

7.17.1.en: St. Anthony the Great: Do not say: "God will look upon the multitude of my offerings, and when I offer them to the Most High He will accept them" [9].

7.17.2.en: God has no need of the offerings and sacrifices that we present; rather the offerings and sacrifices of the Old Testament were symbols of the sacrifice of the Cross that the Messiah the Savior offered for reconciliation. It is a sacrifice of love on the part of the Lord to atone for our sins. As for the sacrifices of praise and thanksgiving that we still offer in the New Testament, in their reality they are a yielding of our bare human will and a thanksgiving to the will of the Lover of mankind, the Savior of the world. Thus offerings and sacrifices in themselves do not bring God's good pleasure, and will not be the object of His delight unless they are offered with faith and trust in God who forgives sins.

7.17.3.en: Do not be fainthearted in your prayer, and do not neglect almsgiving [10].

7.17.4.en: The wise man warns us against our mistaken reliance on almsgiving. For it is not fitting for the believer to do evil relying on the idea that giving many alms will forgive him all the evils he does.

7.17.5.en: The Church took care that she should have her positive and constructive calendar in the life of worship at the daily, weekly, monthly, yearly and jubilee levels, etc., not in dry literal practices, but in living encounters with God and enjoying the pledge of heaven. We mention in a few lines examples of this:

7.17.6.en: The daily level: practicing the canonical hours interacting with personal prayers, in which we remember our life with Him who was born in the manger (the prayer or praise of Prime), and the descent of His Holy Spirit (the praise of the Third Hour), and His crucifixion (the Sixth), and His death for us (the Ninth), and our departure to Him (the Eleventh), and our repose in the Lord (the Twelfth), and our waiting for His last coming (Midnight).

7.17.7.en: The weekly level, such as the fast of Wednesday and Friday, and fellowship in the sacrament of the Eucharist, that is, the Divine Liturgy.

7.17.8.en: The monthly level, such as the celebrations of the feasts of St. Mary and the archangel Michael, etc.

7.17.9.en: The yearly level, such as the feasts of the Lord and the feasts of the saints.

7.17.10.en: The jubilee level, for our renewal by the Spirit of God and tasting godliness.

7.17.11.en: v Hire the poor... and they will prepare for you a high place in the world of light, in which you will lay your treasures. They will build you a great chamber, full of good things, that you may enter it and dwell and find all your treasures. They will be a company surrounding you on the road, and by that great declaration they will ask for you and save you... They will open the door of the Bridegroom before you knock... Be a friend to them so that they may receive you into their tents...

7.18.s.en: 4. Uprightness in speech, work and conduct

7.18.0.en: 12 Do not mock a man in the bitterness of his soul, for there is One who humbles and exalts. 13 Do not devise a lie against your brother, nor contrive it against your friend. 14 Do not desire to lie about anything, for the habit of lying is not for good. 15 Do not multiply words in the assembly of the elders, nor repeat words in your prayer. 16 Do not hate laborious work, nor farming, which the Most High ordained. 17 Do not number yourself among sinners. 18 Remember that wrath does not tarry. 19 Humble yourself greatly, for the punishment of the ungodly is fire and worms. 20 Do not exchange a friend for something temporal, nor a true brother for the gold of Ophir.

7.18.1.en: Since our heavenly Friend calls us to uprightness in our words, works and movements, He came down to us that we may walk in His footsteps, and He even works in us that we may be a living icon of Him in all our conduct. The wise man advises us to righteous conduct and humility. He who mocks a wretched person is foolish, because God who raised you up allowed the other to go down, and He can do the opposite to make a balance [1-6].

7.18.2.en: Vain words without meaning are unfitting in any gatherings with others or in prayer. And manual work was appointed by God for humanity (Gen 2:15; 3:19), and therefore it is honored (38:24-34).

7.19.0.en: The rabbis say that the study of the Torah must be joined with manual work[16]. This is plain in practice from Paul the Apostle and Aquila and Priscilla, since they were tentmakers. In the monastic systems work is counted obligatory for spiritual benefit.

7.19.1.en: Since the Lord reigns over the heart, the soul is filled with the spirit of hope and joy with trust in God's work in it and through it. The believer feels the richness of God's surpassing grace, which makes of him a king with authority even over his thoughts, and he also draws from the wealth of the traits of the incarnate divine Wisdom, so that he walks in a spirit of meekness and humility, and pride has no place in him.

7.19.2.en: Our meeting with the divine Friend, wonderful in His love, fills our inner being, and leads us to walk in heavenly wisdom. This love is reflected in the believer's relation with his brethren, so that he overflows with love toward them in the Lord.

7.19.3.en: Do not mock one who is bitter of soul, for there is One who humbles and exalts [11].

7.19.4.en: Among the most important evils that befall society is making light of one who is bitter of soul. Nothing increases this person's bitterness like mockery of his person, especially if it is because of a personal incapacity in him. It is fitting for the believer to put himself in this person's place and in the same circumstances, and so share the bitterness of his soul, and support him with love and a spirit of hope, and raise him from the bitterness of his life to sweetness. One of the articles of the heavenly Friend's constitution is: "With what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you: and unto you that hear shall more be given" (Mk 4:24). So he who makes light of a person bitter of soul, the bitterness returns to him, and he falls into humiliation, while he who is bitter of soul is exalted. Perhaps by one bitter of soul is meant the person whom want and need have humbled. And as the wise man says: "Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker" (Prov 17:5).

7.19.5.en: "He humbles and exalts", and as Hannah said: "The Lord killeth, and maketh alive: he bringeth down to the grave, and bringeth up. The Lord maketh poor, and maketh rich: he bringeth low, and lifteth up. He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory" (1 Sam 2:6-8). This does not mean that He shows partiality between persons, but as was said by the Virgin Mary: "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree" (Lk 1:52). Christ died once for the whole world, without distinction between classes of people or distinction between races. He offered the Cross for the little infant and the old man, the man and the woman, the Jew and the Gentile.

7.19.6.en: Do not devise a lie against your brother, and do not do the like against your friend [12].

7.19.7.en: The life of society rests on trust among its members, so that all are bound together by the bond of love. The person who slanders his brethren with lies does not deserve to live in society. He commits a hateful crime, because he who does this wrongs the very society that covers the weaknesses of all. He who slanders others falsely is like one who pours deadly poison into society.

7.19.8.en: Beware of every lie, for the habit of it will bring no good [13].

7.19.9.en: The heavenly Friend is the Truth, so he who cleaves to Him does not lie to a neighbor or a friend.

7.19.10.en: Do not speak vanity in the assembly of the elders, and do not repeat words in your prayer [14].

7.20.0.en: He who speaks vanity in the presence of experienced elders sins; how much more he who does so in the presence of God, who searches the hearts and knows the hidden thoughts. This evil comes from the soul's haughtiness and lack of humility [17]. The truly humble person deserves to live in society and to have his constructive effectiveness in the life of his brethren.

7.20.1.en: It is fitting for the believer to sit in the presence of the devout elders to learn, and not to be puffed up with his knowledge, experience and learning.

7.20.2.en: It is fitting for us to control our tongue and sanctify it. For chatter and much talking are snares that the enemy sets so that our tongue may slip and utter vanity. As for prayer, God seeks the fervent heart steadfast in faith, not much speaking and length in prayer.

7.20.3.en: v Wisdom advises us well: "Use not many words in a multitude of elders" (cf. Sir 7:14). Again He asks us to limit vain chatter even in our relation with God by setting a limit with this commandment: "Do not repeat words in vain".

7.20.4.en: St. Clement of Alexandria: Do not hate laborious work, especially farming, which the Most High created [15].

7.20.5.en: Work is a beautiful gift, with many blessings. The Lord Christ says: "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work" (Jn 5:17). And it was said of the angels: "that do his pleasure" (Ps 104). And God created Adam to work in the garden (Gen 3:15). The earnest person does not despise simple tasks, but rejoices if he has the bodily strength to complete them.

7.20.6.en: Do not be prominent in the assembly of sinners, and remember that wrath does not tarry [16].

7.20.7.en: Sitting with sinners exudes upon us their evil traits, and makes us lose calmness of soul and care for our salvation. This is reflected in our thoughts, words and conduct, and brings upon us the curse that awaits them, and since their jesting and sins attract us, we must remember that God's wrath is coming and will not tarry, so that we perish with them. The psalmist takes care for the purity of his life, so he sings: "Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners" (Ps 1:1-2).

7.20.8.en: Humble yourself greatly, for the punishment of the wicked is fire and worms [17].

7.20.9.en: Humbling the soul here is controlling oneself by keeping away from the assemblies of the scornful (Ps 1), for man by nature finds pleasure in practicing sin. When a person humbles himself by repenting of his sins, he escapes eternal judgment.

7.20.10.en: Fire and worms: It was said: "For their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched" (Isa 66:24). The talk here about the worm is a rebuke to sinners who care only for their bodies, for in the end the worm will feed on them.

7.20.11.en: v Sin carries in it the very bread of death, and offers it to those it calls from among the lovers of pleasures and the foolish. "Stolen waters are sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant" (Prov 9:17). As soon as someone touches it, "he knoweth not that the dead are there; and that her guests are in the depths of hell" (cf. Prov 9:18).

7.20.12.en: When a person thinks of tasting pleasure, the outcome of the refreshment in it is not sweet in the end. This is what the wisdom of God affirms: "Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel" (cf. Prov 20:17). And also: "For the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil: But her end is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a twoedged sword" (Prov 5:3-4). So eating of it and enjoying it is for a little while, after that the worm devours him and his soul becomes far away, for the fool does not know that those who are far from God perish[17].

7.21.0.en: St. Athanasius the Apostolic: Do not exchange a friend for money, nor a true brother for the gold of Ophir [18].

7.21.1.en: There is nothing that equals friendship and love, for "charity never faileth" (1 Cor 13:8). One of the grave evils in public life that must be avoided is betrayal of friendship for material gains. Judas became an example of betrayal of friendship for silver, and it was said of him that it would have been good for him if he had not been born (Mt 26:24).

7.21.2.en: Ophir: in the south-west of Arabia, famed as a source of gold in the ancient world. It was said of the Church sitting at the right hand of the Lord Christ: "Upon thy right hand did stand the queen in gold of Ophir" (Ps 45:9).

7.22.0.en: 21 Do not part from your wife, if she is wise and good, for her grace is above gold. 22 Do not mistreat a servant who works faithfully, nor a hired man who gives his life. 23 Let your soul love a wise servant, and do not deny him his freedom. 24 If you have cattle, take care of them, and if they are of use to you, keep them with you. 25 If you have sons, discipline them, and bow down their necks from their youth. 26 If you have daughters, guard their bodies, and do not show a cheerful face to them. 27 Give your daughter in marriage, and you will have accomplished a great matter, and give her to a man of understanding. 28 If you have a wife after your own heart, do not cast her off, but the hated one, do not give yourself to her. 29 Honor your father with all your heart, and do not forget the pangs of your mother. 30 Remember that through them you were born; what can you give them in return for what they have done for you?

7.22.1.en: In speaking of the family, Ben Sirach does not stop at the marriage bond or blood kinship, but commends the servant who works in the family, and the flocks of sheep that the family tends, and the training of the children, and care for their inner peace, and the prevalence of a spirit of faithfulness and sincerity among all, and the honoring of parents.

7.22.2.en: When the Word of God became incarnate and became man, He lived as a child in a humble and holy family. Its relation to Him made it a holy family, and opened the door for every family that He may dwell in its midst and sanctify it. When He says: "The Son of man hath not where to lay his head" (Lk 9:58), He asks us to invite Him to rest in our family, like the house of Mary and Martha and their brother Lazarus, and to lean on His breast with St. John the beloved.

7.22.3.en: Sirach explains with all clarity the obligation toward the members of society: the family, friends, priests and the needy.

7.22.4.en: As for friends, they cannot be exchanged for money. And Ben Sirach also demands good treatment of the faithful servant in the house (33:31-33), and of the laborer (Deut 24:14).

7.22.5.en: The wise servant must be loved by the believer as himself (Lev 19:18), and freedom is to be given to him in the seventh year as the Torah commanded (Ex 21:2; Deut 15:12).

7.22.6.en: Animals had their importance and were a source of wealth for the people, so they must be cared for (Prov 27:23-27).

7.22.7.en: Raising sons requires disciplining them (Prov 13:24), and bowing their necks to the yoke of obedience (30:12-13).

7.22.8.en: Do not disregard a wise and good wife, for her grace is better than gold [19].

7.22.9.en: In speaking of family love, he highlights that marital betrayal is graver than the betrayal of a friend. For if it is fitting for society as a whole to be bound by the bond of faithfulness, sincerity and loyalty to others, how much more must this be observed at the family level through the marriage bond. He who betrays his wife imitates the traitor Judas.

7.22.10.en: The heavenly Friend cares for the wise and good wife, for she enriches the whole family by the grace she enjoys.

7.22.11.en: The talk begins with the good wife as a treasure, whose grace is better than gold. The good wife is able by meekness to win her husband for the heavenly Friend, and she also has priority in influencing the conduct of her sons and daughters.

7.22.12.en: v "Every wise woman buildeth her house: but the foolish plucketh it down with her hands" (Prov 14:1). This means that the wise woman encourages her neighbor in the fear of the Lord and in the love that is in her heart toward her sister and sisters. And on the other hand the foolish woman destroys them with her words full of bitterness, hatred, evil and contempt[18].

7.22.13.en: St. Wisa the Copt: Do not mistreat a servant who works faithfully, nor a hired man who gives himself for you [20].

7.22.14.en: After speaking of the wife, we expected him to speak of the sons and daughters; but he spoke of the faithful servant and the hired man who is earnest in his work and gives himself in his conduct for the master of the house. For the servant and the hired man in the house or in the field leave the imprint of their uprightness on the sons and daughters.
